title: Insights from Volume II of the 1968 Bendix report (Appendices A, B and C)
section: What a simulator user should know about the twelve soils
text:
What a simulator user should know about the twelve soils
Three of the sonic moduli in Table 2-3 of Volume I are estimates, not measurements. The modulus of soil 5 (RSM-a loose) was not measured and the specification estimates it at 7800 psi “based on data for the other soils”; soil 10 (LSM intermediate) was not measured and is estimated at 4000 psi from the LSM value at Dr 0.77 (5000 to 6000 psi); soil 12 (RSM-b dense) was not determined and is estimated at about 20,000 psi. Table 2-3 prints all three as if measured. (A-41, PDF 42; A-79, PDF 80; A-93, PDF 94.)
Loose and dense LSM gave essentially the same friction angle, 40 to 45 degrees, because the loose specimen densified under the normal load before it was sheared; the authors could not draw a phi versus Dr curve for LSM and give a band instead, “the estimated range for Dr .40 to 1.00”. The dilation panels of the LSM data sheets show contraction of 270 thousandths of an inch that is nearly constant with shear displacement, which is the compression under the normal load, not a shear response. A model that sets strength from the as-placed density will misread LSM. (A-79, PDF 80; A-88, PDF 89; Figure C-6B, printed C-18, PDF 132; Figure C-21, printed C-43, PDF 157.)
The wide range and confidence limits of RC2 (soil 6) come from segregation of particle sizes within and between beds, not from degradation: RC2 was shoveled, not vacuumed, so it did not break down, but a broadly graded crushed cinder separates as it is handled. The average grain-size curve combines used and unused soil. (A-49, PDF 50.)
The materials susceptible to breakdown under handling were the cinder soils (RS, PS, RSM-a and RSM-b); the silica sand was not altered by degradation or vacuum handling; RC2 and LSM were shoveled. Each specification states the placement procedure (hopper, number of roller passes per layer), which is the only record of how the beds were built: soil 3 two roller passes, soil 4 sixteen, soil 8 eight, soil 9 twenty-four, soil 12 ten per two inch layer; soils 10 and 11 were “rolled two times (one pass back and forth)” and “six times (three passes back and forth)”. The sheets that count passes never say whether a pass is one direction or a round trip, so the number of times the roller crossed a layer is uncertain by a factor of 2 for soils 3, 4, 8, 9 and 12. (A-24, PDF 25; A-32, PDF 33; A-63, PDF 64; A-70, PDF 71; A-79, PDF 80; A-88, PDF 89; A-93, PDF 94.)
Every specification value, with its page, is in data/materials/specifications.csv, and the generated qa/specifications/table23-vs-appendix-a.md sets each Table 2-3 value beside it: 26 cells differ. The Table 2-3 unit weights reproduce the stated relative densities on the specification density charts within 0.04, except loose SS, whose 94.7 pcf lies below the chart’s minimum density and gives Dr -0.05 (Claude’s arithmetic with Vol. I equation 2-2).
The mixtures are specified by weight: LSM is RC2 cinders and a kaolin-type clay 1:1, RSM-a is cinders and crushed marble 5:7, and RSM-b is cinders and crushed marble 1:3. RSM-a and RSM-b are therefore different materials, not two densities of one material. (A-34, PDF 35; A-73, PDF 74; A-82, PDF 83; A-90, PDF 91.)
The specification text and Table 2-3 disagree on two friction angles: the text gives about 38.3 degrees for soil 11 and about 37 for soil 12, the table 42 and 48; the Appendix A and C curves support the table for soil 12 (about 50 at Dr 1.0) and the discrepancy for soil 11 is unexplained. Soil 12’s placement is also printed differently in the two volumes (10 roller passes per two inch layer in A-93; twenty-four rolls in Volume I printed 2-113). (A-84, PDF 85; A-93, PDF 94.)
The transcription of soils 1 to 6 found more disagreements with Table 2-3. The text gives about 43.9 degrees for soil 3 and 47.9 for soil 4, the table 44.5 and 47.3. Table 2-3 prints one gradation (mean size 1.8 mm, uniformity 1.7, coarseness 2.7 mm) for all four RS and PS rows, while the Appendix A grain size charts give RS a mean size of 2.2 mm and coarseness of 2.8 mm, and PS a uniformity of 1.6. For RC2 the chart prints an average uniformity of “2 5” (range 15-25) and coarseness of 5.0 mm, the table 17.0 and 4.7 mm. Which source is right is not settled by the pages; the measured curves themselves (step 3b) can check it. A user setting up a bed from Table 2-3 should know the table and the specifications differ. (A-6, PDF 7; A-13, PDF 14; A-20, PDF 21; A-28, PDF 29; A-46, PDF 47; Vol. I Table 2-3, printed 2-16, PDF 41; qa/pages-vol2-ab-b2/review.md.)
The silica sand follows the same pattern. The text gives about 29.8 degrees for soil 7, the table 29. The three SS grain size charts give a uniformity of 1.5 and a coarseness of 0.6 mm (range 0.58-0.62), the table 1.3 and 0.52 mm. The table’s unit weight for loose SS, 94.7 pcf, is below every minimum density on the SS density chart (95.0 to 95.8 pcf). (A-52, PDF 53; A-53, PDF 54; A-54, PDF 55; qa/pages-vol2-ab-b3/review.md.)

title: Insights from Volume II of the 1968 Bendix report (Appendices A, B and C)
text:
What the shear data are
Appendix C holds 85 single direct shear tests on 15 soil-and-density series, as data sheets of shear stress and dilation versus shear displacement with the normal stress and unit weight of each test in the legend, plus hand-drawn and computer-fitted failure envelopes. Only one of the 15 series (RS at Dr .50 to .57, Figure C-1B) appears in Volume I (Figure 2-21). The computer fits print “Avg. Density”, “Angle of Friction”, “Tan Theta” and “Cohesion”, and several of the cohesion intercepts are large (700 psf for dense RS) or negative (LSM loose), which says the linear fit is being forced through data that are not linear in normal stress; the hand-drawn envelopes on C-2 to C-21 are the authors’ own reading. (C-1, PDF 115; Figures C-8 to C-15, printed C-24 to C-37, PDF 138 to 151.)
Three of the SS series (Dr .30, .48 and .77) were not run in this study; they are credited to the Bendix interim report MM-65-2 on lunar landing dynamics (as printed on Figure C-5A), which is therefore a source in its own right for silica sand strength. The RSM-b tests (Figure C-7) were run on a different apparatus with loads in psi and no dilation record. (C-1, PDF 115; Figure C-5A, printed C-15, PDF 129; Figures C-7A to C-7C, printed C-21 to C-23, PDF 135 to 137.)

title: Insights from Volume II of the 1968 Bendix report (Appendices A, B and C)
section: What the sonic modulus data are
text:
What the sonic modulus data are
The IITRI measurements (Appendix B) give E = ρc² from a stress-wave velocity in a triaxial specimen confined by partial vacuum, at confining pressures from 0 to about 10 psi, loose and dense, for RS, PS, SS, RC and LSM; there is no RSM measurement. The loose states are Dr 0.30, 0.22, 0.26 and 0.02, not zero. The report calls the LSM results questionable because of a confining pressure gradient in the specimen, and notes that E = ρc² neglects the Poisson factor f(nu), an error under 10 percent for nu below 0.20. (IITRI report M6175, Figures 3 to 8, PDF 109 to 114.)
The “elastic modulus” of Table 2-3 is therefore a small-strain wave modulus, and IITRI says so plainly: moduli from static triaxial tests “will generally differ by an order of magnitude” from wave-velocity values, and dynamic stress-strain curves give values that “may differ by as much as a factor of 4”. The stress wave peaked below 2 psi; loose specimens were poured through a slotted funnel and dense ones vibrated. A simulation that takes E from Table 2-3 is using a wave modulus, not a static one. Under IITRI’s own equation (2), E = ρc² f(nu) with f(nu) at most 1, so ρc² is an upper bound on E for the confined case (Claude’s reading of the printed equations). (Printed 1 to 3, PDF 104 to 106.)
Table 2-3’s moduli at Dr 0, 0.45 and 0.80 were not measured at those densities; IITRI tested RS only at Dr 0.30 and 0.99. Read by eye at 4 psi, the two RS curves give about 7.7 and 12.5 kips/in.², and a straight line in Dr through them gives 5.6, 8.7 and 11.2 at Dr 0, 0.45 and 0.80, close to the table’s 5,500, 8,600 and 10,900 psi. The table looks interpolated and extrapolated in Dr from the IITRI curves; this is an eye reading by Claude, to be confirmed when the curves are read (roadmap step 3b). (Figure 3, printed 6, PDF 109; Vol. I Table 2-3, printed 2-16, PDF 41.)

title: Insights from Volume II of the 1968 Bendix report (Appendices A, B and C)
section: A caution on the appendix pages themselves
text:
A caution on the appendix pages themselves
Two print slips matter to anyone reading the IITRI curves. On Figure 3 (RS) the y tick label between 9 and 7 is printed “3” where 8 belongs, so an axis calibration must not use it. On Figure 5 (SS) the dense label reads “o.84” with a lowercase o for the zero, and the loose label’s “0.” is broken (the value is 0.26). Figure 7 (LSM) includes a specimen at Dr = 1.04, denser than the maximum-density test. (Printed 6, 8 and 10, PDF 109, 111 and 113.)
The Appendix A figures are printed four times per material under new figure numbers (soils 1, 3, 4 share RS; 7, 8, 9 share SS; 10, 11 share LSM), and the “RSM” photomicrograph under soil 12 is the soil 5 photograph reused. The Volcalite chemical analysis is reproduced with two different typesetting slips (A-72, A-81): one gives calcium oxide the magnesium values and drops magnesium, the other gives magnesium oxide the sodium values and drops sodium, and both keep the total 99.25 that their columns no longer reach. The two printings of the clay analysis differ in iron oxide (1.1% on A-72, which matches the 100.0% total; 1.2% on A-81). An agent quoting a value from a specification should quote the first printing of that table (A-2, A-10, A-50, A-72 for the clay) and treat the repeats as copies. (A-72, PDF 73; A-81, PDF 82; A-91, PDF 92.)

title: Terramechanics Reference Data
text:
This site provides laboratory soil tests as numbers: for example, the force needed to push a cylinder into sand as it goes deeper, or the stress at which a soil sample fails in shear. Each test comes with what one would need to set up the same test in a simulator (the soil, how its bed was prepared, the tool and how it moved), and states what the original report leaves out. Every number links to the page of the report it was read from.
This is the beginning of an effort to collect, curate and share well-documented test data that can be used to judge the simulation tools used in terramechanics. To that end, the site also shows how the data are meant to be used with an open-source simulator to gauge its accuracy.
For instance, one set of tests comes from a 1968 NASA study for the Apollo Lunar Module, in which twelve soil conditions were tested on Earth to predict how the lander’s footpads would behave on the Moon.
The collection will grow with further tests, and contributions are welcome of two kinds: data from new physical tests, and scripts that run virtual experiments mirroring the physical tests hosted here.

title: Sonic modulus: LSM soil, Dr = 0.995
text: Sonic modulus test on LSM soil at relative density 0.995; apparatus: shock tube using compressed air; piezoelectric stress gages at each end of a triaxial specimen; oscilloscope arrival times; loading: stress wave from the shock tube driver pressurized to the same pressure each time (peak stress somewhat less than 2 psi); confining pressure by partial vacuum inside a rubber diaphragm. Recorded: modulus vs confining pressure. One of 3 tests drawn from the same figures.

title: Sonic modulus: LSM soil, Dr = 0.995
text:
Data



modulus E = ρc² (wave velocity) against confining pressure, SI units, this test in red and the other tests printed in Fig. B-7 in gray. Error bars are reading bounds (half-widths from the digitization), not standard deviations. Filled markers were agreed by both readings, hollow ones were not.


Peak modulus E = ρc² (wave velocity) 57.89 MPa at 75.5 kPa confining pressure; 57.86 MPa at 75.6 kPa, the end of the record.
Download: observations.csv (21 points: 7 plotted symbols, 10 samples of the drawn curve; columns x_si, y_si with bounds x_bound_si, y_bound_si; panel 1: modulus E = ρc² (wave velocity) in Pa against confining pressure in Pa; the printed-unit values, the pixel position on the scan and the review status of each point are kept in further columns) and series.json (units, conversion factors, how the points were read).
Reading bounds on this figure (how far our reading of the printed figure may be off, not the uncertainty of the test): typical bound 222 Pa in confining pressure, 113.5 kPa in modulus E = ρc² (0.2 percent of the peak). Both independent readings agree within these bounds at 19 of the 21 points; the other 2 were settled against the scan (read by one reader and verified by the other, or decided between two readings). Check the digitized points against the scan.

text: LM model drop (1/6 scale) test on RS soil at relative density 0 to 0.3; apparatus: modified Langley-Grumman 1/6-scale dynamic model of LM (Figs. 5-1 to 5-3); six-degree-of-freedom drop test rig (Figs. 5-12, 5-13) of the Bendix spacecraft model dynamic drop test laboratory (text 5-22); loading: free-body landing after release from the drop rig; total model weight 68.4 Lbs. (text 5-22); zero angular rates, zero pitch and roll, 45-degree yaw, 2-2 landings (text 5-44); level landing surface, zero slope (text 5-43; Table 5-T2); nominal V_v 10 and V_h 0 ft/s for NASA Tests 1, 4 and 6, 5 and 7 ft/s for Tests 2, 3 and 5 (text 5-44, printed teen for ten; Fig. 6-10 gives fps). Recorded: per drop (Table 5-T3): touchdown velocities V_v and V_h, calculated using the measured interval tau between release and ground contact; tau; the bed’s D_r, gamma and phi. Time histories: Section V prints those of NASA Tests 1 and 2 (Figs. 5-22 to 5-39; records b68-mdrop-10, b68-mdrop-11); Section VI plots the measured histories of Tests 1 to 6 against the report’s simulation (Figs. 6-11, 6-13 to 6-17, printed 6-17 to 6-45, PDF 375 to 403), not yet extracted.

title: LM model drop (1/6 scale): RS soil, loose and intermediate, Detail Correlation Drops
text:
Data
Download: runs.csv (6 drops, one physical drop per row: every printed value in SI and as printed, and the record of the drop’s time histories where this collection holds one) and runs.json (units, conversion factors, how the table was read).
The table’s legend: V_v is the vertical velocity, V_h the horizontal velocity, tau the time interval between model release and touchdown, D_r the soil relative density, gamma the soil density (printed in Lb./Ft.^3, a unit weight) and phi the internal angle of friction (Table 5-T3, printed 5-45, PDF 325). The velocities “were calculated based on the exact time interval between the instant of model release to the instant of ground contact”, measured from the readings of the accelerometer in the x direction (printed 5-44, PDF 324), into whose output a pulse was injected at release (printed 5-39, PDF 319); no formula is printed. Signs are as printed; the report’s fixed axes point up from the ground and along the horizontal velocity (printed 5-18, PDF 298). Every drop had zero angular rates, zero pitch and roll and a 45-degree yaw (a 2-2 landing) (printed 5-44, PDF 324), on a level bed (printed 5-43, PDF 323). A new bed was prepared for every drop; dynamic penetrometer readings were taken on it after the drop, away from the footpads, and the report points to the correlation of D_r with those readings (Paragraph 2.7.1) and to Section II for the other properties (printed 5-44, PDF 324). Section V prints the time histories of NASA Tests No. 1 and 2 (Figs. 5-22 to 5-39); Section VI plots the measured histories of all eight drops against the report’s computer simulation (Figs. 6-11 and 6-13 to 6-19, printed 6-17 to 6-53, PDF 375 to 411), with the drop conditions again in Fig. 6-10 (printed 6-15, PDF 373).
Our arithmetic, not the report’s, over all 8 drops of the table, against |V_v| = g tau (the speed of a free fall from rest over tau) within the rounding of both printed numbers. With the report’s g for Earth, 32.2 ft/s² (9.81456 m/s²; glossary, printed 2-2, PDF 27), 3 of the 4 vertical drops (V_h 0) and 0 of the 4 drops with a horizontal velocity are consistent with it; with standard gravity, 9.80665 m/s², 4 of 4 and 1 of 4 (NASA Test No. 3). The two values of g differ by 0.08 percent, about the rounding of a printed tau, so at this precision the verdicts depend on the g used. This shows consistency, not the method, which the report does not state.
Time histories: NASA Test No. 1 in b68-mdrop-10; NASA Test No. 2 in b68-mdrop-11; for the other drops they are not yet extracted (the report plots them against its simulation in Section VI).

title: LM model drop (1/6 scale): RS soil, loose, NASA Test No. 1
text:
Data



footpad penetration depth and axial load, strut No. 3 and axial load, strut No. 2 and axial load, strut No. 1 against time, SI units. Error bars are reading bounds (half-widths from the digitization), not standard deviations. Filled markers were agreed by both readings, hollow ones were not.


Peak footpad penetration depth 112.57 mm at 80 ms time; 109.87 mm at 99.8 ms, the end of the record. Axial load, strut No. 3 3.306 N at the end. Axial load, strut No. 2 42.83 N at the end. Axial load, strut No. 1 -20.21 N at the end.
Download: observations.csv (207 points: 0 plotted symbols, 178 samples of the drawn curve; columns x_si, y_si with bounds x_bound_si, y_bound_si; panel 1 (Fig. 5-24): footpad penetration depth in m against time in s; panel 2 (Fig. 5-25): axial load, strut No. 3 in N against time in s; panel 3 (Fig. 5-25): axial load, strut No. 2 in N against time in s; panel 4 (Fig. 5-25): axial load, strut No. 1 in N against time in s; the printed-unit values, the pixel position on the scan and the review status of each point are kept in further columns) and series.json (units, conversion factors, how the points were read).
Reading bounds on these figures (how far our reading of the printed figure may be off, not the uncertainty of the test): typical bound 0.22 ms in time, 551 micrometers in footpad penetration depth (Fig. 5-24) (0.5 percent of the peak), 3.722 N in axial load, strut No. 3 (Fig. 5-25), 3.948 N in axial load, strut No. 2 (Fig. 5-25), 4.001 N in axial load, strut No. 1 (Fig. 5-25). Both independent readings agree within these bounds at 196 of the 207 points; 4 are still under review (hollow in the plot) and 7 were settled against the scan. Check the digitized points against the scan: F5-24, F5-25.
About these values. No. 1 footpad of the 1/6-scale model, NASA Test No. 1. The depth is a computed output, not a direct measurement: the report’s data reduction program took the 13 tape-recorded signals every 1/1000 s and calculated the footpad’s penetration by numerical integration (AM-68-1 Vol. I, Section 5.5.2, printed 5-41, PDF 321). Axial load of the strut, tension positive and compression negative, as the panel’s printed labels give it (the axis title names the sense of the trace’s main excursion); a trace beyond the panel’s 0 line changes sense. On the Strut No. 2 panel the top load label is printed -60; the panel’s own sequence (0, +20, +40) and the (Tension) title make it +60, and both readings anchor that line at +60 lbf. Where the scan has no ink the line is left open: a break in the drawn line at about 0.0138 to 0.0140 s, about 4 px of the page with no ink, the line resuming about 1.5 px to the side.

title: Load-penetration test (LPT) 24: 4-inch (102 mm) cylinder pushed into dense red scoria (RS)
text: A cylinder 101.6 mm (4 in) in diameter was pushed into a bed of dense red scoria (RS), and the load on it was recorded against its penetration. This is a load-penetration test (LPT), run at 0.423 mm/s in a bed of bulk density 825 kg/m³.

title: Load-penetration test (LPT) 24: 4-inch (102 mm) cylinder pushed into dense red scoria (RS)
text:
Virtual experiment card
What one would need to set up the same test in a simulator. Each value carries one of three marks: reported given by the report for this test or its apparatus, or for the procedure of these tests in general where the text says so; soil reference a property of the soil from another table of the report, for the soil’s nominal state; left to the user an input the report does not give, with what it says around it. Each citation opens the page of the report, AM-68-1 Volume I unless noted: the printed page number, then the page of the PDF file in parentheses.






what the record gives
where printed




Soil
reported red crushed volcanic scoria, narrowly graded (RS), dense; printed as RS Dense
Fig. 2-42, p. 2-77 (PDF 102); Fig. 2-44, p. 2-79 (PDF 104)



reported bulk density 825 kg/m³ (unit weight 51.5 pcf as printed)
Fig. 2-42, p. 2-77 (PDF 102)



reported dynamic penetrometer reading (Gp) 83 g
Fig. 2-42, p. 2-77 (PDF 102); Fig. 2-44, p. 2-79 (PDF 104)



soil reference soil No. 4 of the report’s soil table, RS Dense (matched to the test by the soil and its state, not printed with it), at its nominal state: relative density 0.80, bulk density 810.5 kg/m³, mean grain size (D50) 1.8 mm, uniformity coefficient (Cu) 1.7, 95 percent size (D95) 2.7 mm, fines (finer than 0.075 mm) under 3 percent
Table 2-3, p. 2-16 (PDF 41)



soil reference at that nominal state: friction angle 47.3 degrees (direct shear); modulus 75.2 MPa, measured with sound waves at 27.6 kPa (4 psi) confinement. The report warns that static and wave-based moduli can differ by an order of magnitude
Table 2-3, p. 2-16 (PDF 41); Vol. II, App. B, p. 1 (PDF 104)



soil reference air dried, as were all the test soils: 0.2 to 0.3 percent water by weight, occasionally 0.6
p. 2-103 (PDF 128)


Bed
reported bin 0.457 m by 0.914 m in plan (18 by 36 in as printed)
Fig. 2-44, p. 2-79 (PDF 104)



reported the load-penetration bin: a box of 25 mm (1 in) plywood, 0.457 m wide, 0.914 m long and 0.914 m deep, with a front of plate glass 25 mm (1 in) thick and 0.457 m (18 in) deep, standing on load cells that weigh the soil
Sec. 2.6.1, p. 2-56 (PDF 81)


Tool
reported cylinder, 101.6 mm (4 in) in diameter, pushed down into the bed by a hydraulic cylinder
Fig. 2-42, p. 2-77 (PDF 102); Fig. 2-44, p. 2-79 (PDF 104); Sec. 2.6.1, p. 2-56 (PDF 81)



reported in the standard setup the nearest wall of the bin is 229 mm (9 in, 4.5 radii) from the axis of a 101.6 mm cylinder, so the cylinder sits midway across the bin’s width
p. 2-59 (PDF 84)


Motion
reported starts at the soil surface (start depth 0 in the test’s record)




reported pushed at a constant 0.423 mm/s (1 in/min as printed); the operator keeps the rate by making the plotting pen follow a line of penetration against time
Fig. 2-42, p. 2-77 (PDF 102); p. 2-57 (PDF 82); p. 2-59 (PDF 84)



reported the procedure pushes the cylinder 203 mm (8 in), or until the hydraulic supply reaches its capacity; how far this test went is not printed
p. 2-59 (PDF 84)


Environment
reported laboratory test on Earth




reported gravity: 9.81456 m/s², the report’s value for Earth, 32.2 ft/s², converted exactly
glossary, p. 2-2 (PDF 27)


Measured
reported the load on the cylinder, from the test load cell, against its penetration, from a stroke wire, both drawn by an x-y plotter
Sec. 2.6.1, p. 2-56 (PDF 81)



reported the printed curve, read into the data, runs from 1.3 to 74.0 mm of penetration (where it meets the frame of the plot)
Fig. 2-42, p. 2-77 (PDF 102)


Missing: choices left to the user
left to the user fill depth: not printed. The procedure fills the box in stages and weighs the bed at six volume marks up to the full box (13.78 cubic feet, 0.390 m³) to check that its density is uniform
Sec. 2.6.2, p. 2-57 (PDF 82)



left to the user how the bed was placed and compacted: not printed for this test. The dense beds of these tests were generally made with a vibratory plate compactor, three passes per layer about 76 mm (3 in) thick, giving relative densities of 0.85 to 0.95
p. 2-113 (PDF 138)



left to the user the zero of penetration: the printed load leaves zero at 1.3 mm; whether the cylinder touched the surface there or at zero is not stated
Fig. 2-42, p. 2-77 (PDF 102)



left to the user relative density of this bed: not printed. The tests of Fig. 2-44, this one among them, average about 0.96. Read at this bed’s density on the report’s density chart for the soil, it is about 0.90 (0.82 to above 1 within the chart’s 95 percent limits). The soil table’s 0.80 belongs to the soil’s nominal state, not to this bed
Fig. 2-44, p. 2-79 (PDF 104); p. 2-74 (PDF 99); Vol. II, Fig. A-3, p. A-7 (PDF 8); Table 2-3, p. 2-16 (PDF 41)



left to the user soil strength at this bed’s density: the report plots friction angle against relative density
Fig. 2-23, p. 2-46 (PDF 71)



left to the user cohesion: a bearing-capacity interpretation in the report, not a measured input. It found that the apparent cohesion of its shear tests predicts higher bearing loads than observed, and that about 0.7 kPa (0.1 psi), some 50 times less, explains some of the size effects in these tests
p. 2-47 (PDF 72)



left to the user the cylinder’s end shape, length, material and surface, and where it stood along the bin: not printed




left to the user friction between the soil and the cylinder, and between the soil and the walls (plywood, glass): not reported




left to the user any model parameter the report does not measure, such as a static stiffness or the properties of grains






Codes on this card: RS, red crushed volcanic scoria, narrowly graded; Gp, peak deceleration of the dynamic penetrometer, in g; D50, grain size that half of the soil, by weight, is finer than; D95, grain size that 95 percent of the soil, by weight, is finer than; Cu, uniformity coefficient.
A simulation of this test is compared with the measurement through the axial force the soil exerts on the cylinder, the force the load cell measured, against the cylinder’s penetration below the original soil surface. A comparison states where it puts the zero of force and of penetration, and whether the cylinder’s own weight is included. The Simulate a test page walks through the steps.

title: Load-penetration test (LPT) 24: 4-inch (102 mm) cylinder pushed into dense red scoria (RS)
text:
Measured data



Load against penetration: this test in red, the other tests printed in Fig. 2-42 in gray. The error bars on the red curve are its reading bounds. The round markers are the curve’s marked features (start, peaks, troughs, end); filled ones were agreed by both readings, hollow ones were not. The two hollow markers near 39 mm are competing readings of the same trough, still being settled; they are one feature, not two. Click to enlarge.


Download the points (CSV) Download the reading record (JSON)
The CSV file gives penetration in m (x_si) and load in N (y_si), each with its reading bound (x_bound_si, y_bound_si), and the status of each point. The JSON file gives the units, the conversion factors and how the points were read. A reading bound says how precisely a point could be read from the printed figure, typically 0.55 mm in penetration and 21 N in load here. It is not the scatter of the experiment, which the report does not give. Both readings drawn over the scanned figure.

title: Footpad impact: RS soil, dense, Run No. 12
text:
Data



vertical force against time; displacement against time; vertical force against displacement, SI units, this test in red and the other tests printed in Fig. 4-19 in gray. Error bars are reading bounds (half-widths from the digitization), not standard deviations. Filled markers were agreed by both readings, hollow ones were not.


Peak vertical force 2616 N at 4.29 ms time; 118.2 N at 130 ms, the end of the record. Displacement 31.35 mm at the end.
Download: observations.csv (198 points: 0 plotted symbols, 180 samples of the drawn curve; columns x_si, y_si with bounds x_bound_si, y_bound_si; panel 1 (Fig. 4-19): vertical force in N against time in s; panel 2 (Fig. 4-19): displacement in m against time in s; panel 3 (Fig. 4-20): vertical force in N against displacement in m; the printed-unit values, the pixel position on the scan and the review status of each point are kept in further columns) and series.json (units, conversion factors, how the points were read).
Reading bounds on these figures (how far our reading of the printed figure may be off, not the uncertainty of the test): typical bound 0.789 ms in time, typical bound 333 micrometers in displacement, 17.4 N in vertical force (Fig. 4-19) (0.7 percent of the peak), 669 micrometers in displacement (Fig. 4-19), 15.16 N in vertical force (Fig. 4-20). Both independent readings agree within these bounds at 144 of the 198 points; 17 are still under review (hollow in the plot) and 37 were settled against the scan. Check the digitized points against the scan: F4-19, F4-20.
About these values. Past 100 ms the printed time labels skip 110: the evenly spaced lines after the 100 ms line are labeled 120, 130 and 140 and the frame after them is unlabeled. The values read those lines as 110, 120 and 130 ms and the frame as 140 ms, from the even spacing. Taken as printed, a time between the 100 ms line and the next would be up to 10 ms later (the difference grows across that interval) and every later time 10 ms later. Fig. 4-20 cannot test this: the same rescaling of both time axes leaves force against displacement unchanged. Fig. 4-20 plots the force of panel 1 against the displacement of panel 2: the same runs, cross-plotted from the same records.

title: Dynamic penetration (DPT): RS soil, intermediate, Record No. 54025
text:

deceleration against time, SI units, this test in red and the other tests printed in Fig. 2-54 in gray. Error bars are reading bounds (half-widths from the digitization), not standard deviations. Filled markers were agreed by both readings, hollow ones were not.

Download: observations.csv (100 points: 0 plotted symbols, 89 samples of the drawn curve; columns x_si, y_si with bounds x_bound_si, y_bound_si; panel 1 (Fig. 2-54): deceleration in m/s^2 against time in s; the printed-unit values, the pixel position on the scan and the review status of each point are kept in further columns) and series.json (units, conversion factors, how the points were read).

The figure prints no time origin: time is counted from the timing line that carries the three deceleration rulers (0 ms), so only differences of time are measured; the timing lines are 10 ms apart (the figure’s 0.01 s bar). Deceleration is in g as printed (G’s), positive upward, converted with standard gravity; 0 g is each ruler’s printed zero, not the dashed line drawn about 0.7 to 1.0 g above it. Samples are in drawing order and may share a time on a steep flank.

title: Density measurement: PS soil, loose, Density Versus Relative Density for PS Soil
text:
Data



unit weight (minimum at Dr 0 to maximum at Dr 1.0) against relative density, SI units. Error bars are reading bounds (half-widths from the digitization), not standard deviations. Filled markers were agreed by both readings, hollow ones were not.


Peak unit weight (minimum at Dr 0 to maximum at Dr 1.0) 4743 N/m^3 at 1 relative density; 4746 N/m^3 at 1, the end of the record.
Download: observations.csv (38 points: 0 plotted symbols, 32 samples of the drawn curve; columns x_si, y_si with bounds x_bound_si, y_bound_si; panel 1: unit weight (minimum at Dr 0 to maximum at Dr 1.0) in N/m^3 against relative density (dimensionless); the printed-unit values, the pixel position on the scan and the review status of each point are kept in further columns) and series.json (units, conversion factors, how the points were read).
Reading bounds on this figure (how far our reading of the printed figure may be off, not the uncertainty of the test): typical bound 0.003552 in relative density, 9.011 N/m^3 in unit weight (0.2 percent of the peak). Both independent readings agree within these bounds at 33 of the 38 points; 2 are still under review (hollow in the plot) and 3 were settled against the scan. Check the digitized points against the scan.

title: Contribute
text: The collection is open to contributions of two kinds, and to corrections. The maintainers review each one; once accepted, it is credited and listed in the changelog of the release that adds it.

title: Contribute
Contribute
section: A script that runs a virtual experiment

title: Contribute
text:
Corrections
A point that looks wrong, a better scan of a page, or an answer to one of the open questions (under Project records): give the page and, for a point, where it is on the scan. For a value that looks wrong, the Report a problem with a value form asks for the release, the record id, the figure or table, the printed and PDF pages, and the evidence.

title: Contribute
section: How to send it, and how it is reviewed
text:
How to send it, and how it is reviewed
Open an issue on the project’s GitHub repository. The maintainers check data against its source, and run a script to confirm that it gives the output it states. Accepted contributions enter under the same rules as everything else here: every number traceable to its source. Feedback not meant to be public goes to Dan Negrut, negrut@wisc.edu.

title: About
text: Terramechanics Reference Data collects measured soil tests and the setup of each, so that a simulation of the same test can be compared with the measurement. It is maintained by the Simulation-Based Engineering Laboratory (SBEL), University of Wisconsin-Madison.

title: About
text:
Sources
The tests come from published reports. Those in this release come from the Bendix “Lunar Module (LM) Soil Mechanics Study” (NASA, 1968, report AM-68-1), in two volumes: Volume I, Sections II to V (soil selection and the basic tests, the drag and impact tests, and the 1/6-scale Lunar Module model drops) and Volume II, Appendices A to C (soil specifications, sonic moduli and the full direct shear program). NASA’s technical reports server lists it for public distribution, with public use permitted. The page images on this site come from it, courtesy of NASA; the report itself is linked, not copied: Volume I and Volume II (D-054). The Sources page lists the 7 reports acquired for the collection and the leads being considered.

title: About
section: How the numbers were read and checked
text:
How the numbers were read and checked
Most numbers in the reports exist only as printed figures. Each figure whose numbers are in the data was read twice, separately, by two readers (the AI systems Claude and Codex), each from the scanned page and without seeing the other’s reading. In some early batches both readers also saw notes from an earlier step, so those readings were not fully independent; the review record of each batch says where. A script compared the two readings point by point. Where they disagreed, a fresh reading of the page, made without knowing which reading was whose, settled it, or the point was left marked as unsettled. Then student reviewers compare a sample of the points with the scan, and every check they make is recorded.
Every point carries:

its source: the report, the figure or table, the printed page and the page of the PDF file;
a reading bound: how precisely it could be read from the printed figure (not the scatter of the experiment, which the reports rarely give);
a status word that says which of the checks above it passed (see the Glossary).

Values are given in SI units, with the printed value kept beside them. On the Figures page both readings are drawn over the scanned page, so any point can be checked by eye. The detailed rules are in Methods.

title: About
text:
Known limitations

The numbers are read from scans more than half a century old; each point’s reading bound says how precisely.
The reports rarely give the uncertainty of the experiments themselves. Tests repeated on similar beds show how much results can differ.
Some setups are incomplete: the depth of a soil bed, or how it was placed, is often not printed. Each test page lists what is missing as choices left to the user.
Only a sample of the points is checked by a person; each test page says how many.
Where the report contradicts itself (a test labeled differently in two figures), the record says so rather than choosing. The open questions, under Project records, list every such case.

title: About
text:
Using the data

Find a test: Find a test lists every record; each test’s page gives its setup, its plot and its source pages.
Download its values: the buttons under the plot give the points in SI (CSV) and how they were read (JSON); Download gives the index files.
Trace a number: each value names the report, figure or table, printed page and PDF page; the scanned page is on the test’s page, and the Figures page draws the readings over it.
Cite it: the release used, the record id, and the page of the report (each test’s page shows how).

title: About
text:
Contribute, cite, follow the work

Contribute: data from new tests, scripts that run virtual experiments, corrections.
Download: the files, the license and how to cite.
Project records: decisions, the review record and the open questions.

title: Decisions
text:
The decisions that shaped the method, oldest first, under the numbers the data and the documents cite. Decisions about the people and the logistics of the review are summarized.

D-001
2026-10-07
Which Chrono soil model family is validated first?
CRM first then DEM; DEM first; both at once
CRM first; DEM later


D-002
2026-10-07
Which test families are in scope for the first benchmark?
static only; static plus dynamic penetration; everything
Static tests plus dynamic penetration (DPT and impacts); drag provisional


D-003
2026-10-07
Which soil families are extracted?
RS and SS only; all six families
All six families (twelve soils of Table 2-3)


D-004
2026-10-07
Where does the work live and who sees it?
public repo now; private until submission
Private repository DanNegrut/terramech-appolo-data until the data paper is submitted; release-ready from day one


D-005
2026-10-07
What does the student review?
everything; disagreements only; disagreements plus an audit sample
Disagreements only; plus a 5 to 10 percent audit of agreements (added after Codex’s plan review)


D-006
2026-10-07
Which CRM rheology is the baseline?
mu(I); MCC; both
mu(I) baseline; MCC enters only if a test demands history dependence


D-007
2026-10-07
How is in_scope defined in the figures index?
narrow (numbers to extract); broad (worth transcribing); two columns
Two columns: in_scope narrow plus transcribe yes for all of Section II


D-008
2026-10-07
Which priority rule do the indexes use?
protocol-based; Claude’s as filed; Codex’s as filed
Protocol-based: 1 needed for the first calibration and prediction protocols; 2 setup and interpretation; 3 context


D-009
2026-10-07
What does mcc_relevant mean?
narrow (history dependence shown); broad (anything touching density or compaction); drop
Narrow: same material after different histories with a different response; plus the state maps needed to read them


D-010
2026-10-07
What comes after the Section II indexes?
Volume II Appendices A and C inventory; Section II transcription; Section IV inventory
Appendix C and A inventory first; page-diff tool piloted on five Section II pages; then Section II transcription


D-011
2026-10-07
Should the source hunt be broadened beyond the Bendix lineage?
Bendix lineage only; all public-domain granular test records usable for simulator validation
Broadened: Apollo era to today; declared scope per release; eligibility graded on rights; data form and setup recoverability


D-012
2026-10-07
Should the project have a website and how?
one page; generated Quarto site; other generator; web app
Generated Quarto website; pages written by tools/build_site.py from the repository; nothing hand-edited; provenance and status on every display


D-013
2026-10-07
Are generated site pages committed?
committed; build output only
Committed; deterministic generator; byte-for-byte regeneration check; commit hash injected at render time


D-014
2026-10-07
What must accompany every reported result on the site?
plot and CSV only; plot plus provenance; plus the full setup needed to run the experiment in a simulator
Provenance to the page image (overlay of extracted points; pixel coordinates and anchors) and a Reproduce-this-experiment block with material; state; strength; geometry; loading; measurement and what is missing


D-015
2026-10-07
Apollo-era sources only or also later simulant data?
Apollo era only; also later simulant data (GRC-1 and JSC-1A and successors)
open


D-016
2026-10-07
How are Volume II unnumbered tables and repeated figures indexed?
one row per soil specification; one row per printed table with a page-locator id; repeats dropped
One row per printed table with id TA-pNNN (PDF page); repeated figures and tables kept as rows with relation reproduces and in_scope no and priority 3; relations to Volume I recorded (derived-from and reproduces)


D-017
2026-10-08
When does the first paper go out and how does the validation effort split?
data paper after the simulations; data paper as soon as the harvest and website are done; one validation thread; CRM and DEM threads
Data paper as soon as the harvest is reviewed and the website UX is iterated (no simulation result needed); validation then runs as two parallel threads with their own papers: CRM (mu(I) baseline per D-006) and DEM; framing is archaeology of half-century-old test data made public for sim2real


D-018
2026-10-08
How are two trace readings sampled at different displacements compared and how wide is a trace bound?
nearest-x matching with x treated as a measurement; interpolate the other reading at the canonical sample and compare y with the slope-propagated x bounds; bound = full line thickness; bound = half the line thickness
Interpolation rule with slope-propagated x bounds; trace bound is half the line thickness (center known to within half the width); one-sided points enter data only as one-sided-verified after the other agent checks the page or stay one-sided; interpolations across visible gaps are excluded


D-019
2026-10-08
What does a record page show and where does the maintainers’ material go?
one page with everything (status table, reconciliation record, agents’ notes, data); user-facing page with the process material collapsed; user-facing page with the process material on a separate provenance page
Record pages carry only what a user of the data needs (summary, trust note, data in SI, reproduce table with as-printed values and per-test-type fields, family, source pages, citation); the reconciliation record, point statuses, calibration residuals, agents’ notes and audit status live on review/; scan overlays once per figure on the figures page; persistent ambiguities that matter for reproduction are stated on the page and labeled as our observation; the pilot’s wide bounds stay until a re-read after the student audit


D-020
2026-10-08
How are student audits organized?
one packet per student with announced checks; unannounced seeded mistakes; single or double review per point
A light starter packet first (8 rows), identical for every student; seeded attention checks in every packet, whose answers are known, never announced and scored before any answer is recorded; every audited point reviewed by two students (four students, six pairs cycled); no time estimate given to students


D-021
2026-10-09
How does a checklist row tell the student what to do, and how does the student look closer?
guide only; a question per row in the checklist; value columns kept or dropped; an image viewer to install; a viewer page in the packet
Each checklist row states its question in a ‘what to check’ column; the value columns (value read, other reading) are dropped because the answer comes from the picture; a compare row is answered in A with blue, orange or cannot tell; compare close-ups show a wider window (3x, 300 scan px) so both curves’ symbols are in view; every packet carries viewer.html (the scan in a browser page, offline: pick a row or type pixel x and y to place the crosshair, pixel under the mouse)


D-022
2026-10-13
How is the full audit of the digitized figures organized?
one e-mail with everything once all data exists; weekly waves as the data is read; fixed pairs or rotating pairs; 2 or 5 hours a week
Weekly waves, each with the figures read that week and due a week later; every chunk to one pair of reviewers, the pairs cycled so that each person gets about 4 chunks of about 60 rows a week and no fixed partner; seeded attention checks in every chunk; sampling per figure: compare rows (cap 6), all resolved and unverified one-sided points, one-sided-verified points (cap 10), then agreed points round-robin to a quota proportional to the square root of the figure’s point count; answer keys never in a packet; scoring chunk by chunk across runs, with a status board.


D-023
2026-10-13
How are two curve readings reconciled when they differ in what they cover, and who settles disputed points?
pair markers by sequence or by position; bridge gaps in the other trace under a pixel threshold or verify by eye; compare features by position or by role; keep or drop points only the non-canonical reader recorded; one adjudicator or two blind ones
Markers paired by position on the page; features by role (first, peak, last) and a peak compared in y only with its x bound widened to the other reading; trace samples inside a gap of the other trace stay one-sided and are verified by eye, no bridging rule; points only the non-canonical reader recorded are kept as one-sided with their own source; a one-sided marker on another test’s marker in the other reading is an identity conflict; every disputed or one-sided point goes to a blind adjudication packet (neutral labels P and Q), answered independently by a Claude and a Codex adjudicator; agreement settles, the other agent’s adjudicator verifies one-sided points, splits go to a second round and then to the human audit


D-024
2026-10-14
Five method questions from batches curves-appc-b3 to -b5: calibration of gridless figures, triangle centers, envelope identity, a printed legend error, re-deriving values after a tool fix
residual rule as is or limited to printed anchors; bounding-box center or centroid; line or legend shape for identity; keep or correct a printed legend; re-read or re-derive
A calibration residual counts only against printed marks (detected grid lines or measured ticks); residuals over lines predicted from the frame show internal consistency and cannot win the canonical choice, so a batch may name the canonical reading with its reason (overlays.csv canonical, canonical_reason); a reader who saved a tick map is re-derived on it so both compete on printed marks. Triangle center: the centroid of the reconstructed triangle; until the 1968 registration point is established the bound in the apex direction includes the bounding-box midpoint (height/6); earlier readings with mixed conventions are to be normalized by a documented re-derivation (open). Envelope identity: neither line nor shape decides alone; the data-sheet peaks of the same tests, where they distinguish the candidates, settle it (corroboration from another depiction, not independent validation). A printed legend error is corrected by a canonical-stage series rename with its evidence (series-ids.csv), the submissions and *_printed fields faithful to the print. Values re-derived from a submission’s own pixels and calibration after a tool fix are sound and kept under qa//rederived/.


D-025
2026-10-14
One affine map per panel, or a piecewise map between the drawn lines, on hand-drafted grids that are not uniform?
affine over all lines; affine over the labelled lines only; piecewise linear between verified lines
Piecewise linear between verified scale lines on every panel (no threshold: on a uniform grid it equals the affine map), in the axis’s transformed coordinates for log scales, keeping each line’s tilt. A frame is a knot only with a supported value (on FC-6B and FC-6D the left frame is x = 0, recorded as inferred: the first lower-panel symbols sit on it); predicted lines and misplaced text are never knots. Bounds propagate the point’s pixel interval and the position intervals of its two bracketing lines, with line-location error from independent checks; the global affine residual becomes a diagnostic of the drafting and is no longer added to every point. The two readings’ maps are compared at every knot and interval over the plot, not only at four corners, and the canonical reading is chosen by independent line-position validation (tie to the first submission). The affine-minus-piecewise difference is reported as a correlated calibration sensitivity (initial stiffness above all); slope changes at grid lines are not soil behaviour. Existing readings: pixels kept, values re-derived under qa//rederived/, reconciliation rerun, ink and identity decisions carried by source and sequence. To be implemented in tools/calibrate_axes.py, diff_curves.py and build_observations.py as one step, then all batches re-derived (open).


D-026
2026-10-14
D-025 as implemented: how is a reader’s line verified against the page, which reading is canonical when the ink cannot separate the maps, and what happens to earlier decisions when the canonical reading changes?
tie: first submission, previous canonical reader, denser sampling, affine residual; decisions: re-adjudicate everything, carry by neighbourhood, carry through the pairing; line check: median distance, ink-line fit over the line’s length
Tie: first submission (Claude), within 0.25 px of mean line distance from the ink; recomputable from the submissions, the page and the recovered lines, unlike the previous reader, and not a measure of sampling effort or of the retired residual. The authors of CITATION.cff are also the Zenodo creators and appear in the site’s search metadata (extends D-051). Contact: negrut@wisc.edu and GitHub issues. Until 12-03 only site fixes; a data correction becomes v1.0.1.


D-053
2026-11-23
Is a late return of a withdrawn chunk recorded (D-047)?
(a) record a late return whose attention checks all pass, as its chunk’s second review, and withdraw a later chunk that asks the same points again; (b) keep D-047 as written: not recorded
(a). A late return of a withdrawn chunk is recorded as its chunk’s second review when every attention check in it passes, and a later chunk that asks the same points again is withdrawn before any answer; a late return that misses a check is declined. D-047’s reason, that the old packets predate the current guide and tools, does not make such answers weaker than the first reviews they pair with, which were made with the same packets and guide.


D-054
2026-11-23
Does the public release copy the NASA reports (PDF files) or link to them?
(a) link: leave the reports from NASA’s Technical Reports Server out of the public repository and the Zenodo deposit, each one’s NTRS link and SHA-256 in sources/register.csv; (b) copy them, as D-034 planned
(a). The five reports from NASA’s Technical Reports Server (AM-68-1 Volumes I and II, NASA-CR-66914, WES M-71-10 Reports 1 and 2) stay out of the public release; sources/register.csv gives each one’s NTRS link, the file name the tools expect and the SHA-256 of the copy that was read, so a reader can fetch and verify it. NASA’s reuse page allows documents without a copyright notice to be reproduced and distributed, with NASA acknowledged, but its API terms ask that the citation link be used instead of a full-text copy whenever possible, and that copies of a record that becomes unavailable be removed, which a Zenodo deposit and a public history cannot do. The Planetary Data System bundles (public domain) stay in. The page images on the site, single pages shown as evidence, stay, credited to NASA. Amends D-034, under which the tracked sources went in so that every page image could be rendered from the release alone: that now takes one download per report.


D-055
2026-11-25
Who are the data set’s authors (CITATION.cff and the Zenodo creators), and how are the people whose work enters a release credited as the data set grows?
(a) every person whose work enters a release becomes an author of the data set (D-051); (b) the authors are the people responsible for the data set over time, the lab’s two co-leaders; everyone else whose work enters a release is named on that version’s Zenodo record as a contributor with a role, and each data paper, a snapshot, is authored by the people who did the work it describes
(b), from v1.0.0. The authors are Dan Negrut and Radu Serban, co-leaders of SBEL, who share responsibility for the data set’s releases and upkeep; CITATION.cff and the Zenodo creators list them in that order. The student reviewers are named on the Zenodo record of each version that holds their work as contributors with the role data curator, and are co-authors of the data paper of 12-18 (D-048). The contributor list is cumulative: nobody is removed from a later version. As the data set grows, update papers describe it, each authored by the people who did the work since the paper before. A student reviewer who asks to stay an author of version 1.0.0 stays an author of that version only. Amends D-051 (reviewers named in the data set’s author list) and D-052 (the authors of CITATION.cff are the Zenodo creators; the contributors appear on the Zenodo record only).


D-056
2026-11-25
Where is the data paper submitted, and what question does it answer?
(a) Scientific Data, as a Data Descriptor (D-048); (b) Journal of Terramechanics, as a research article on what the 1968 tests tell us and how far to trust them, with the data set as its deliverable, and Scientific Data as the fallback
(b). The paper goes to the Journal of Terramechanics, submitted 2026-12-18 with an arXiv copy the same day. It is written as a research article whose question is what the 1968 tests tell us and how far to trust them: the test-to-test spread that the report’s repeated tests show (LPT 23 and LPT 24, run at the same rate and within 1 pcf, differ by about 20% in load), what each test’s recorded setup fixes and what it leaves open, what a study needs to know to choose its calibration and held-out tests (D-028), and how accurately the printed figures were recovered (two blind AI readings compared mechanically, people checking a sample of every figure, stated as in D-050). The data set, cited by its DOI, is the paper’s deliverable; the paper carries no simulation result (D-045). Elsevier’s template and a research article’s structure replace the Data Descriptor layout. Scientific Data, as a Data Descriptor, is the fallback if the Journal of Terramechanics declines the paper. Amends D-048.


D-057
2026-11-25
How do the paper and the data set relate as the data set grows, and when do the WES wheel tests enter?
(a) one schedule: new sources wait until after the paper (D-049); (b) the paper describes a frozen version and the data set keeps growing in versioned releases; the WES wheel tables enter now, before any human check, labeled as such
(b). The paper describes the 1968 records of v1.2.0 and cites its version DOI; the website and the data set keep growing in releases, each with a Zenodo DOI. A new source enters under the rules of AGENTS.md: two independent readings, a mechanical diff, disagreements settled by a blind re-reading of the scan or left pending-review with the SI value empty; never a single reading. Its human checks follow; until then every page and download of the source says ‘Two independent AI transcriptions, compared. Human check pending. People have checked k of N values; K values unresolved’, with the counts generated from the records. Versions: v1.0.0 (11-28), the 1968 records; v1.1.0 (12-04 or 12-05), the first tables of the WES wheel tests (U.S. Army Waterways Experiment Station, M-71-10 Reports 1 and 2), the firm scope being Report 2 Tables 8, 4 and 1 with the wheel descriptions and test setup, Table 7 a stretch; v1.2.0 (12-08), the paper’s version, with the human checks and the WES tables finished by then; v1.3.0 (January), the second reviews and the human checks of the WES tables. Nothing new is public before 12-04 (D-052). The paper’s statement of human checks (D-050) is computed over the 1968 records of v1.2.0. The data record no calibration or held-out roles for the WES tests (D-028). Amends D-049 and D-050: the paper cites v1.2.0, frozen 12-08, not v1.1.


D-058
2026-11-27
Does v1.0.0 go public on Saturday 11-28, as planned (D-052), or a day early?
(a) as planned: data and review status frozen Friday 11-27 at noon, public Saturday 11-28; (b) public Friday 11-27, with the freeze made that morning
(b). Data and review status are frozen on the morning of Friday 11-27 and v1.0.0 is published that day; CITATION.cff gives 2026-11-27 as the release date. The rest of D-052 holds: the partner email on 12-03, nothing new public before 12-04, and a data correction before then becomes v1.0.1. Supersedes the dates of v1.0.0 in D-052 (public on Saturday 11-28, freeze at noon on 11-27) and in D-057.

title: Dynamic penetration (DPT): RS soil, Record No. 54-65 LPT No. 26
text:
Data



deceleration against time, SI units. Error bars are reading bounds (half-widths from the digitization), not standard deviations. Filled markers were agreed by both readings, hollow ones were not.


Peak deceleration 763.1 m/s^2 at 14.8 ms time; 12.81 m/s^2 at 88 ms, the end of the record.
Download: observations.csv (109 points: 0 plotted symbols, 102 samples of the drawn curve; columns x_si, y_si with bounds x_bound_si, y_bound_si; panel 1 (Fig. 2-54): deceleration in m/s^2 against time in s; the printed-unit values, the pixel position on the scan and the review status of each point are kept in further columns) and series.json (units, conversion factors, how the points were read).
Reading bounds on this figure (how far our reading of the printed figure may be off, not the uncertainty of the test): typical bound 0.356 ms in time, 4.79 m/s^2 in deceleration (Fig. 2-54) (0.6 percent of the peak). Both independent readings agree within these bounds at 102 of the 109 points; the other 7 were settled against the scan (read by one reader and verified by the other, or decided between two readings). Check the digitized points against the scan.
About these values. The figure prints no time origin: time is counted from the timing line that carries the three deceleration rulers (0 ms), so only differences of time are measured; the timing lines are 10 ms apart (the figure’s 0.01 s bar). Deceleration is in g as printed (G’s), positive upward, converted with standard gravity; 0 g is each ruler’s printed zero, not the dashed line drawn about 0.7 to 1.0 g above it. Samples are in drawing order and may share a time on a steep flank.

text:
Data
Download: runs.csv (32 runs, one physical test per row: every printed value in SI and as printed, the four derived columns the report prints, and the arithmetic check of each row) and runs.json (units, conversion factors, how the table was read).
The report defines the areas in the derived columns only by name (A_ft the total horizontal frontal area, A_pt the vertical frontal area of the footpad, Fig. 4-4); the depth d is measured from the soil surface to the bottom of the pad at zero pitch. Checked against each other, the two pressure columns agree only with a common factor of 0.9738 to 0.9763, which every run fits: the factor a unit weight of 40.02 to 40.13 rather than the printed 41.1 pcf would give in the authors’ arithmetic; which input differs, the page does not say. text: Direct shear test on RS soil (Red Crushed Volcanic Scoria (narrowly graded)) at relative density 0.5 to 0.57; apparatus: direct shear box 2-1/2 inch diameter; loading: shear at constant normal stress 1172 psf. Recorded: shear stress and normal displacement vs shear displacement. One of 7 tests of this soil and density at normal stresses from 14.1 to 168.5 kPa, the family the report used to draw the failure envelope.

title: Direct shear of RS soil at 56.1 kPa normal stress
text:
Data



shear stress and dilation (normal displacement; positive up) against shear displacement, SI units, this test in red and the other tests printed in Fig. C-1B in gray. Error bars are reading bounds (half-widths from the digitization), not standard deviations. Filled markers were agreed by both readings, hollow ones were not.


Peak shear stress 83.6 kPa at 2.92 mm shear displacement; 73.5 kPa at 6.37 mm, the end of the record. Dilation 1.57 mm at the end.
Download: observations.csv (78 points: 26 plotted symbols, 49 samples of the drawn curve; columns x_si, y_si with bounds x_bound_si, y_bound_si; panel 1: shear stress in Pa against shear displacement in m; panel 2: dilation (normal displacement; positive up) in m against shear displacement in m; the printed-unit values, the pixel position on the scan and the review status of each point are kept in further columns) and series.json (units, conversion factors, how the points were read).
Reading bounds on this figure (how far our reading of the printed figure may be off, not the uncertainty of the test): typical bound 8 micrometers in shear displacement, 1.2 kPa in shear stress (1.5 percent of the peak), 33 micrometers in dilation. Both independent readings agree within these bounds at 36 of the 78 points; 23 are still under review (hollow in the plot) and 19 were settled against the scan. Check the digitized points against the scan.

Recorded: vertical force vs time; displacement vs time; vertical force vs displacement. One of 2 tests drawn from the same figures.

title: Footpad impact: RS soil, intermediate, Run No. 10
text:
Data



vertical force against time; displacement against time; vertical force against displacement, SI units, this test in red and the other tests printed in Fig. 4-19 in gray. Error bars are reading bounds (half-widths from the digitization), not standard deviations. Filled markers were agreed by both readings, hollow ones were not.


Peak vertical force 1264 N at 3.68 ms time; 136.7 N at 130 ms, the end of the record. Displacement 50.60 mm at the end.
Download: observations.csv (142 points: 0 plotted symbols, 124 samples of the drawn curve; columns x_si, y_si with bounds x_bound_si, y_bound_si; panel 1 (Fig. 4-19): vertical force in N against time in s; panel 2 (Fig. 4-19): displacement in m against time in s; panel 3 (Fig. 4-20): vertical force in N against displacement in m; the printed-unit values, the pixel position on the scan and the review status of each point are kept in further columns) and series.json (units, conversion factors, how the points were read).
Reading bounds on these figures (how far our reading of the printed figure may be off, not the uncertainty of the test): typical bound 0.603 ms in time, typical bound 275 micrometers in displacement, 13.43 N in vertical force (Fig. 4-19) (1.1 percent of the peak), 706 micrometers in displacement (Fig. 4-19), 8.411 N in vertical force (Fig. 4-20). Both independent readings agree within these bounds at 128 of the 142 points; 3 are still under review (hollow in the plot) and 11 were settled against the scan. Check the digitized points against the scan: F4-19, F4-20.
About these values. Past 100 ms the printed time labels skip 110: the evenly spaced lines after the 100 ms line are labeled 120, 130 and 140 and the frame after them is unlabeled. The values read those lines as 110, 120 and 130 ms and the frame as 140 ms, from the even spacing. Taken as printed, a time between the 100 ms line and the next would be up to 10 ms later (the difference grows across that interval) and every later time 10 ms later. Fig. 4-20 cannot test this: the same rescaling of both time axes leaves force against displacement unchanged. Fig. 4-20 plots the force of panel 1 against the displacement of panel 2: the same runs, cross-plotted from the same records. Where the scan has no ink the line is left open: scan dropout: no ink, grid lines included, from about 1.61 to 1.92 in (both readers stop at the last dot before it and resume after it).

title: Footpad impact: RS soil, loose, Run No. 4
text:
Data



vertical force against time; displacement against time; vertical force against displacement, SI units. Error bars are reading bounds (half-widths from the digitization), not standard deviations. Filled markers were agreed by both readings, hollow ones were not.


Peak vertical force 634.7 N at 74.7 ms time; 204 N at 130 ms, the end of the record. Displacement 104.72 mm at the end.
Download: observations.csv (167 points: 0 plotted symbols, 147 samples of the drawn curve; columns x_si, y_si with bounds x_bound_si, y_bound_si; panel 1 (Fig. 4-19): vertical force in N against time in s; panel 2 (Fig. 4-19): displacement in m against time in s; panel 3 (Fig. 4-20): vertical force in N against displacement in m; the printed-unit values, the pixel position on the scan and the review status of each point are kept in further columns) and series.json (units, conversion factors, how the points were read).
Reading bounds on these figures (how far our reading of the printed figure may be off, not the uncertainty of the test): typical bound 0.546 ms in time, typical bound 276 micrometers in displacement, 13.67 N in vertical force (Fig. 4-19) (2.2 percent of the peak), 776 micrometers in displacement (Fig. 4-19), 9.36 N in vertical force (Fig. 4-20). Both independent readings agree within these bounds at 158 of the 167 points; 1 is still under review (hollow in the plot) and 8 were settled against the scan. Check the digitized points against the scan: F4-19, F4-20.
About these values. Past 100 ms the printed time labels skip 110: the evenly spaced lines after the 100 ms line are labeled 120, 130 and 140 and the frame after them is unlabeled. The values read those lines as 110, 120 and 130 ms and the frame as 140 ms, from the even spacing. Taken as printed, a time between the 100 ms line and the next would be up to 10 ms later (the difference grows across that interval) and every later time 10 ms later. Fig. 4-20 cannot test this: the same rescaling of both time axes leaves force against displacement unchanged. Fig. 4-20 plots the force of panel 1 against the displacement of panel 2: the same runs, cross-plotted from the same records. Where the scan has no ink the line is left open: scan dropout: no ink from about 1.78 to 1.84 in (both readers).

title: LM model drop (1/6 scale): RS soil, loose, NASA Test No. 2
text: LM model drop (1/6 scale) test on RS soil (Red Crushed Volcanic Scoria (narrowly graded)) at relative density 0; apparatus: modified 1/6-scale LM model; six-degree-of-freedom drop test rig; loading: free drop; Total Model Weight 68.4 Lbs.; yaw 45 deg (2-2 landing), zero pitch and roll, zero angular rates; level surface (ground slope 0). Recorded: absolute footpad velocity VAP vs time; footpad heading theta vs time; footpad penetration depth vs time; strut No. 1 axial load vs time; strut No. 2 axial load vs time; strut No. 3 axial load vs time; CG vertical acceleration vs time; CG vertical velocity vs time; CG vertical displacement vs time; CG horizontal velocity vs time; CG horizontal displacement vs time; vehicle pitch velocity vs time; vehicle pitch angle vs time.

title: LM model drop (1/6 scale): RS soil, loose, NASA Test No. 2
text:
Data



footpad penetration depth and axial load, strut No. 3 and axial load, strut No. 2 and axial load, strut No. 1 against time, SI units. Error bars are reading bounds (half-widths from the digitization), not standard deviations. Filled markers were agreed by both readings, hollow ones were not.


Peak footpad penetration depth 106.90 mm at 99.6 ms time, the end of the record. Axial load, strut No. 3 -106.9 N at the end. Axial load, strut No. 2 224.6 N at the end. Axial load, strut No. 1 -225 N at the end.
Download: observations.csv (170 points: 0 plotted symbols, 142 samples of the drawn curve; columns x_si, y_si with bounds x_bound_si, y_bound_si; panel 1 (Fig. 5-31): footpad penetration depth in m against time in s; panel 2 (Fig. 5-32): axial load, strut No. 3 in N against time in s; panel 3 (Fig. 5-32): axial load, strut No. 2 in N against time in s; panel 4 (Fig. 5-32): axial load, strut No. 1 in N against time in s; the printed-unit values, the pixel position on the scan and the review status of each point are kept in further columns) and series.json (units, conversion factors, how the points were read).
Reading bounds on these figures (how far our reading of the printed figure may be off, not the uncertainty of the test): typical bound 0.211 ms in time, 572 micrometers in footpad penetration depth (Fig. 5-31) (0.5 percent of the peak), 4.254 N in axial load, strut No. 3 (Fig. 5-32), 3.776 N in axial load, strut No. 2 (Fig. 5-32), 4.225 N in axial load, strut No. 1 (Fig. 5-32). Both independent readings agree within these bounds at 156 of the 170 points; 6 are still under review (hollow in the plot) and 8 were settled against the scan. Check the digitized points against the scan: F5-31, F5-32.
About these values. No. 1 footpad of the 1/6-scale model, NASA Test No. 2. The depth is a computed output, not a direct measurement: the report’s data reduction program took the 13 tape-recorded signals every 1/1000 s and calculated the footpad’s penetration by numerical integration (AM-68-1 Vol. I, Section 5.5.2, printed 5-41, PDF 321). Axial load of the strut, tension positive and compression negative, as the panel’s printed labels give it (the axis title names the sense of the trace’s main excursion); a trace beyond the panel’s 0 line changes sense. On Fig. 5-32, past 0.09 s the time is extrapolated: the 0.10 s line is too faint on the scan to anchor, and the three strut traces end at about 0.103 s in both readings. On the Strut No. 2 panel the top load label is printed -60; the panel’s own sequence (0, +20, +40) and the (Tension) title make it +60, and both readings anchor that line at +60 lbf. Where the scan has no ink the line is left open: a break in the drawn line at about 0.0089 to 0.0091 s, about 4 px of the page with no ink; a break in the drawn line at about 0.0261 to 0.0263 s, about 4 px of the page with no ink.

title: LM model drop (1/6 scale): SS soil, loose, Detail Correlation Drops
text:
Data
Download: runs.csv (2 drops, one physical drop per row: every printed value in SI and as printed, and the record of the drop’s time histories where this collection holds one) and runs.json (units, conversion factors, how the table was read).
The table’s legend: V_v is the vertical velocity, V_h the horizontal velocity, tau the time interval between model release and touchdown, D_r the soil relative density, gamma the soil density (printed in Lb./Ft.^3, a unit weight) and phi the internal angle of friction (Table 5-T3, printed 5-45, PDF 325). The velocities “were calculated based on the exact time interval between the instant of model release to the instant of ground contact”, measured from the readings of the accelerometer in the x direction (printed 5-44, PDF 324), into whose output a pulse was injected at release (printed 5-39, PDF 319); no formula is printed. Signs are as printed; the report’s fixed axes point up from the ground and along the horizontal velocity (printed 5-18, PDF 298). Every drop had zero angular rates, zero pitch and roll and a 45-degree yaw (a 2-2 landing) (printed 5-44, PDF 324), on a level bed (printed 5-43, PDF 323). A new bed was prepared for every drop; dynamic penetrometer readings were taken on it after the drop, away from the footpads, and the report points to the correlation of D_r with those readings (Paragraph 2.7.1) and to Section II for the other properties (printed 5-44, PDF 324). Section V prints the time histories of NASA Tests No. 1 and 2 (Figs. 5-22 to 5-39); Section VI plots the measured histories of all eight drops against the report’s computer simulation (Figs. 6-11 and 6-13 to 6-19, printed 6-17 to 6-53, PDF 375 to 411), with the drop conditions again in Fig. 6-10 (printed 6-15, PDF 373).
Our arithmetic, not the report’s, over all 8 drops of the table, against |V_v| = g tau (the speed of a free fall from rest over tau) within the rounding of both printed numbers. With the report’s g for Earth, 32.2 ft/s² (9.81456 m/s²; glossary, printed 2-2, PDF 27), 3 of the 4 vertical drops (V_h 0) and 0 of the 4 drops with a horizontal velocity are consistent with it; with standard gravity, 9.80665 m/s², 4 of 4 and 1 of 4 (NASA Test No. 3). The two values of g differ by 0.08 percent, about the rounding of a printed tau, so at this precision the verdicts depend on the g used. This shows consistency, not the method, which the report does not state.
Time histories of these drops: not yet extracted (the report plots them against its simulation in Section VI).

title: Sonic modulus: RS soil, Dense, Dr = 0.99
text: Sonic modulus test on RS soil at relative density 0.99; apparatus: shock tube using compressed air; piezoelectric stress gages at each end of a triaxial specimen; oscilloscope arrival times; loading: stress wave from the shock tube driver pressurized to the same pressure each time (peak stress somewhat less than 2 psi); confining pressure by partial vacuum inside a rubber diaphragm. Recorded: modulus vs confining pressure. One of 2 tests drawn from the same figures.

title: Sonic modulus: RS soil, Dense, Dr = 0.99
text:
Data



modulus E = ρc² (wave velocity) against confining pressure, SI units, this test in red and the other tests printed in Fig. B-3 in gray. Error bars are reading bounds (half-widths from the digitization), not standard deviations. Filled markers were agreed by both readings, hollow ones were not.


Peak modulus E = ρc² (wave velocity) 121.42 MPa at 66.9 kPa confining pressure; 121.52 MPa at 67.1 kPa, the end of the record.
Download: observations.csv (22 points: 6 plotted symbols, 13 samples of the drawn curve; columns x_si, y_si with bounds x_bound_si, y_bound_si; panel 1: modulus E = ρc² (wave velocity) in Pa against confining pressure in Pa; the printed-unit values, the pixel position on the scan and the review status of each point are kept in further columns) and series.json (units, conversion factors, how the points were read).
Reading bounds on this figure (how far our reading of the printed figure may be off, not the uncertainty of the test): typical bound 304 Pa in confining pressure, 123.9 kPa in modulus E = ρc² (0.1 percent of the peak). Both independent readings agree within these bounds at 15 of the 22 points; the other 7 were settled against the scan (read by one reader and verified by the other, or decided between two readings). Check the digitized points against the scan.

title: Sonic modulus: SS soil, Dense, Dr = o.84
text: Sonic modulus test on SS soil at relative density o.84; apparatus: shock tube using compressed air; piezoelectric stress gages at each end of a triaxial specimen; oscilloscope arrival times; loading: stress wave from the shock tube driver pressurized to the same pressure each time (peak stress somewhat less than 2 psi); confining pressure by partial vacuum inside a rubber diaphragm. Recorded: modulus vs confining pressure. One of 2 tests drawn from the same figures.

title: Sonic modulus: SS soil, Dense, Dr = o.84
text:
Data



modulus E = ρc² (wave velocity) against confining pressure, SI units, this test in red and the other tests printed in Fig. B-5 in gray. Error bars are reading bounds (half-widths from the digitization), not standard deviations. Filled markers were agreed by both readings, hollow ones were not.


Peak modulus E = ρc² (wave velocity) 256.34 MPa at 67.3 kPa confining pressure; 256.96 MPa at 67.5 kPa, the end of the record.
Download: observations.csv (21 points: 7 plotted symbols, 11 samples of the drawn curve; columns x_si, y_si with bounds x_bound_si, y_bound_si; panel 1: modulus E = ρc² (wave velocity) in Pa against confining pressure in Pa; the printed-unit values, the pixel position on the scan and the review status of each point are kept in further columns) and series.json (units, conversion factors, how the points were read).
Reading bounds on this figure (how far our reading of the printed figure may be off, not the uncertainty of the test): typical bound 188 Pa in confining pressure, 373.4 kPa in modulus E = ρc² (0.1 percent of the peak). Both independent readings agree within these bounds at 17 of the 21 points; 2 are still under review (hollow in the plot) and 2 were settled against the scan. Check the digitized points against the scan.
