title: Glossary
text: The codes, symbols and status words used on the pages for readers of this site. Where the 1968 report defines a term itself, its own definition is quoted with the page it is printed on.

title: Glossary
text:
Soils










code
soil
the report’s definition
where printed




RS
red crushed volcanic scoria, narrowly graded
Red narrowly-graded crushed volcanic scoria; one of the basic soil types used in the LM SMS.
AM-68-1 Vol. I, printed 2-3, PDF 28


PS
white crushed pumice, narrowly graded
White narrowly graded crushed pumice; a basic test soil type used in the LM SMS.
AM-68-1 Vol. I, printed 2-3, PDF 28


RSM-a
RS mixed with crushed marble, 5 to 7 by weight, narrowly graded
A narrowly-graded mixture of five parts of RS material and seven parts of crushed marble by weight; one of the basic soil types used in the LM SMS.
AM-68-1 Vol. I, printed 2-3, PDF 28


RSM-b
RS mixed with crushed marble, 1 to 3 by weight, narrowly graded
A narrowly-graded mixture of one part of RS material and three parts of crushed marble by weight; one of the basic soil types used in the LM SMS.
AM-68-1 Vol. I, printed 2-3, PDF 28


RC2
red crushed volcanic scoria, broadly graded
Red broadly-graded “crusher run” andesitic volcanic scoria; one of the basic soil types used in the LM SMS. It was obtained from the same source as the RS material.
AM-68-1 Vol. I, printed 2-3, PDF 28


SS
white silica sand (Wedron 4040), narrowly graded
White Silica Sand (Wedron 4040-narrowly graded)
AM-68-1 Vol. I, Table 2-3, printed 2-16, PDF 41


LSM
broadly graded scoria (RC2) mixed with air-floated clay
A basic test soil type used in the LM SMS; a mixture of crushed volcanic scoria (RC2) and air-floated clay designed to simulate certain features of the lunar soil as indicated by the Surveyor I photographs.
AM-68-1 Vol. I, printed 2-2, PDF 27




A narrowly graded soil has grains of nearly one size; a broadly graded one mixes a wide range of sizes. RSM stands for either mixture of RS and crushed marble. The report’s soil table gives each soil at one or more states, numbered 1 to 12 (the Soils page). In the report’s definitions, LM SMS is the study itself: the Lunar Excursion Module Soil Mechanics Study (AM-68-1 Vol. I, printed 2-2, PDF 27).

title: Glossary
text:
Soil states
A state is a range of relative density (Dr): 0 at the soil’s loosest reference state and 1 at its densest reference state (the maximum and minimum void ratios found by the minimum-maximum density tests); a bed packed past the densest reference state reads above 1.









state
the report’s definition
where printed




loose
Loose; describing a soil in a loose state of compaction; a soil for which \(0.0 ≤ D_r ≤ 0.3\).
AM-68-1 Vol. I, printed 2-2, PDF 27


intermediate
Intermediate; describing a soil in an intermediate state of compaction; a soil for which \(0.3 ≤ D_r ≤ 0.7\).
AM-68-1 Vol. I, printed 2-2, PDF 27


dense
Dense (i.e. describing a soil in a dense state of compaction; a soil for which \(0.7 ≤ D_r ≤ 1.0\)).
AM-68-1 Vol. I, printed 2-2, PDF 27

title: Glossary
text:
Test types









code on this site
test
what is measured




lpt
load-penetration test, LPT
the load on a tool (a cylinder or a footpad) pushed into a soil bed, against how deep it has gone


ds
direct shear test
the shear stress that makes a soil sample slide along a plane, at a set normal stress, and how much the sample swells or shrinks


dpt
dynamic penetrometer test, DPT
the peak deceleration of a probe dropped into the bed, Gp


dens
density test
the density a soil reaches with a given compaction, or its loosest and densest states


gs
grain size analysis
the fraction of the soil, by weight, finer than each sieve size


sonic
sonic modulus test
the stiffness of a soil sample from the speed of a sound wave through it


tx
triaxial test
the strength of a soil cylinder under a confining pressure

title: Glossary
text:
Symbols









symbol
meaning
where the report defines it




Dr
relative density: 0 at the soil’s maximum void ratio (loosest reference state), 1 at its minimum (densest reference state); computed from the void ratio and those two limits, so a bed packed past the densest reference state reads above 1 (Vol. II reports up to 1.16)
AM-68-1 Vol. I, printed 2-29, PDF 54


unit weight, γ
weight of soil per unit volume; the report prints it in pcf (pounds per cubic foot). This site gives the bulk density, mass per unit volume, in kg/m³
AM-68-1 Vol. I, printed 2-60, PDF 85


friction angle, φ
the angle of internal friction of the soil, from the direct shear tests
AM-68-1 Vol. I, printed 2-11, PDF 36


E
elastic (Young’s) modulus
AM-68-1 Vol. I, printed 2-11, PDF 36



the soil table’s modulus is measured by sonic means at 27.6 kPa (4 psi) confinement
AM-68-1 Vol. I, Table 2-3, printed 2-16, PDF 41


C
cohesive strength, as used in the bearing capacity equation
AM-68-1 Vol. I, printed 2-60, PDF 85



the report found the apparent cohesion from its shear tests too large to match its bearing tests
AM-68-1 Vol. I, printed 2-47, PDF 72


Gp
peak deceleration of the dynamic penetrometer, in g (one g is 9.81 m/s²)
AM-68-1 Vol. I, Fig. 2-52, printed 2-89, PDF 114


D50
mean grain size: the grain size that half of the soil, by weight, is finer than
AM-68-1 Vol. I, printed 2-26, PDF 51


D10
effective size: the grain size that 10 percent of the soil, by weight, is finer than
AM-68-1 Vol. I, printed 2-26, PDF 51


D60
the grain size that 60 percent of the soil, by weight, is finer than
AM-68-1 Vol. I, printed 2-26, PDF 51


Cu
uniformity coefficient, D60 divided by D10; near 1 for a narrowly graded soil
AM-68-1 Vol. I, printed 2-26, PDF 51


D95
the grain size that 95 percent of the soil, by weight, is finer than
AM-68-1 Vol. I, Table 2-3, printed 2-16, PDF 41

title: Glossary
text:
Status words
Each point of data carries one status, which says how it was checked.








status
meaning




agreed
the two readings, made separately, matched within their reading bounds


resolved
the readings differed, and a further reading of the page settled which was right


one-sided-verified
only one reading has the point, and the other reader confirmed it on the page


one-sided
only one reading has the point, and the other reader has not confirmed it; a person may or may not have checked it (audited and confirmed say so)


pending-review
unsettled; not yet decided


audited
the readings agreed, and two student reviewers also confirmed the point on the scan


confirmed
the point rested on a rule, a further reading or one reading, and two student reviewers confirmed it on the scan




The lists of tests and soils also carry a status for each row of the index, built the same way: agreed, normalized (matched once units or spelling were made the same), resolved or resolved-with-notes (settled by a further reading, with a note), rule or convention (settled by a documented rule), provisional (a count to be redone), conflict (the report gives two different values) and one-sided.
A reading bound is how precisely a point could be read from the printed figure: a half-width, not a standard deviation, and not the uncertainty of the experiment.

title: Glossary
text:
Missing values
A value the data do not have is never shown as a blank or a zero, but as one of these:








shown as
meaning




not reported
the report does not give it


not yet extracted
the report gives it, but it is not in the data yet


unreadable
the scan does not allow a reading


conflicting evidence
the report gives two different values


not applicable
the quantity has no meaning for this test

title: Glossary
text:
Kinds of record









kind
meaning
an independent test?




single
one physical test on one soil bed
yes


averaged-series
a curve the report says is averaged from several tests
no


derived-series
a result the authors drew from identified tests, such as a failure envelope from several shear tests
no


correlation
a fitted curve drawn without the points behind it

title: Insights from Section II of the 1968 Bendix report (soil selection and control)
text:
Note



Review status: pending. Written from a first read of the pages; quote with that caveat until the page transcriptions are reconciled.
Judgment, caveats and recommendations the authors recorded, as distinct from the numbers. Each paragraph ends with its citation (AM-68-1 Vol. I, printed page, PDF page). Written 2026-10-07 from a first read of the pages; review_status: pending until the transcription is reconciled.

title: Insights from Section II of the 1968 Bendix report (soil selection and control)
text:
Why these soils
The test soils were chosen to span target ranges set from Surveyor-era estimates of lunar soil: density 20 to 110 pcf, relative density 0 to near 100 percent, friction angle 25 to over 50 degrees, cohesion 0 to under 100 psf, mean grain size under 70 to 2000 microns. The soils were then paired so that one property at a time could be isolated: PS loose against RS loose isolates bulk density (same gradation and friction, very different density); RS loose, intermediate and dense isolate relative density; the SS series does the same for a silica sand. (Table 2-1, printed 2-12, PDF 37; Figure 2-7, printed 2-17, PDF 42.)
The report’s own soil model deliberately includes no strain-rate property: the force on a footpad is written as a function of unit weight, friction, relative density, modulus, cohesion and friction angle only. Rate effects were examined separately in the load-penetration tests and found small up to 4 inches per minute. (printed 2-10, PDF 35; printed 2-74, PDF 99.)

title: Insights from Section II of the 1968 Bendix report (soil selection and control)
text:
Density and bed preparation
Relative density is defined through the minimum and maximum density test (Burmister funnel method for minimum; vibratory compaction in 1 inch layers for maximum), and unit weight is linear in 1/gamma against Dr, which is why Figure 2-17 is drawn on a reciprocal scale. Acceptance of a determination required values within 3 percent of the average. (printed 2-29 to 2-35, PDF 54 to 60.)
Bed preparation is a first-order effect and the report says so repeatedly. Loose beds (Dr near 0) came from a traveling hopper whose trailing edge rides at the soil surface, designed because screeding a loose surface densifies it; scoop placing gives Dr about 0.15; slope filling segregates coarse and fine grains. Intermediate beds came from screeding thin layers (small LPT bin) or from a lawn roller with a soil-specific number of passes (soil 3: two rolls per layer, Dr about 0.4; soil 8: eight rolls, Dr about 0.6; soil 10: two rolls under cardboard, Dr about 0.5). Dense LPT beds came from a vibratory plate, three passes per 3 inch layer, Dr 0.85 to 0.95; dense beds in the large bins from the roller (soil 4: sixteen rolls, Dr about 0.7; soil 9: twenty-four, Dr 0.75 to 0.8; soil 11: six under cardboard, Dr about 0.7; soil 12: twenty-four, Dr about 0.78). A simulation that claims to reproduce a test must reproduce the stated Dr of that bed, not the nominal state name. (printed 2-103 to 2-113, PDF 128 to 138.)
All soils were tested air dried; moisture 0.2 to 0.3 percent, occasionally 0.6. (printed 2-103, PDF 128.)

title: Insights from Section II of the 1968 Bendix report (soil selection and control)
section: The soils degraded during the campaign
text:
The soils degraded during the campaign
The cinder soils (RS, PS, RSM) broke down when handled through the vacuum system used to empty and fill the drag and impact bins; RS and RSM significantly, PS less, SS not at all, and LSM and RC2 were shoveled to protect their fines. Minimum and maximum densities rose with the number of vacuum cycles: for RS from 41.1/53.6 pcf unused to 63.6/76.6 pcf after 46 cycles. Figure 2-60 shows the slope of the density trend increasing after test 1-75, when the vacuum system came into use, while DPT-derived relative density stayed roughly uniform. Consequence: the RS soil in a late drag test is not the RS soil of Table 2-3, and any simulation of a drag or impact test must use the density limits of the bed on that date, which the report tabulates by test number. (printed 2-94 to 2-98, PDF 119 to 123; printed 2-101 to 2-102, PDF 126 to 127.)

title: Insights from Section II of the 1968 Bendix report (soil selection and control)
section: Direct shear results and their interpretation
text:
Direct shear results and their interpretation
Friction angles of the cinder soils are substantially higher than those of silica sand (29 to 41 degrees for SS against 39 to 53 for the cinders), and their failure envelopes show appreciable apparent cohesion. The authors attribute the high friction to particle angularity and surface roughness, and the apparent cohesion to interlocking or to particle crushing at higher normal stress (their Figure 2-25 hypothesis). They did not use apparent cohesion as a soil descriptor because it did not correlate with static and dynamic strength. (printed 2-45 to 2-52, PDF 70 to 77.)
A footnote gives the number that matters for calibration: a cohesion of about 0.1 psi explains the size effects seen in the load-penetration tests, while the apparent cohesion from direct shear was about 50 times larger. Putting the direct-shear cohesion into Terzaghi’s equation over-predicts bearing strength. (printed 2-47, PDF 72.)
The LSM soil shows no change of friction angle with relative density because the loose LSM densified under the normal load before shearing; its curve in Figure 2-23 is built from the lowest normal loads only. Relative density in the shear tests is the value before the normal load was applied. (printed 2-45 footnote and 2-52, PDF 70 and 77.)
Triaxial tests were few, on RS intermediate and dense only, and gave friction angles of about 38 degrees, or 39 and 43 degrees at low confining pressure and 36 at high when re-examined for crushing. One direct shear series on RS at Dr about 1.0 gave 52.6 degrees against the 49.5 used as the dense RS average. (printed 2-49, PDF 74; printed 2-66 footnote, PDF 91.)

title: Insights from Section II of the 1968 Bendix report (soil selection and control)
text:
Load-penetration tests
The LPT bin is 18 by 36 by 36 inches with a glass front, on load cells so the bed weight and hence unit weight are known per volume increment. Cylinders of 1, 2, 4 and 8 inch diameter and footpads of 4 and 6.17 inch were pushed at controlled rates to 8 inches or hydraulic capacity. (printed 2-56 to 2-59, PDF 81 to 84.)
Boundary effects were real: in dense SS a failure plane reached the glass face of the 18 inch bin, so tests were repeated in 36 by 36, 54 by 36 and 108 by 36 inch bins. Larger bins gave higher peak loads and lower post-failure slopes; the small bin raised the apparent Nq by about 50 percent for a 1.5 degree change in friction angle. This sets the minimum domain size for a virtual experiment and warns that the 18 inch bin results for dense soils carry a boundary signature. (printed 2-59, 2-68 and 2-74, PDF 84, 93 and 99.)
The dimensionless pressure parameter q/(D gamma) against relative depth Df/D collapses tests of different cylinder size onto one curve for loose and intermediate RS (Dr 0 to 0.7), but not for dense soils, where smaller cylinders read higher; the 1 inch cylinder much higher. The authors conclude that the size effect implied by the bearing capacity equation fails for small cylinders in dense soil. A pronounced dip in one intermediate curve is attributed to screeding as the placement method. (printed 2-69, PDF 94.)
Footpad curves lie below cylinder curves at the same depth; the authors give three reasons: lower average depth of the dished pad, no side friction, and soil falling in above the pad. (printed 2-80, PDF 105.)

title: Insights from Section II of the 1968 Bendix report (soil selection and control)
section: The dynamic penetrometer and inferred density
text:
The dynamic penetrometer and inferred density
The DPT is a 1.59 lb, 2-3/4 inch aluminum body with a full-radius nose and a 100 g accelerometer, dropped 25.4 inches through a guide tube. Peak deceleration Gp was correlated against directly measured relative density in calibration bins (Figure 2-55) and then used to assign Dr to beds where density could not be measured directly, that is, most drag and impact beds. Two caveats from the authors: calibration bins could not reach Gp values as low as the drag and impact bins did, so the hopper placed soil looser than the minimum density test, or the calibration bins had boundary effects; and in-place density scoop readings scattered and read low. Any validation against a DPT inferred density is therefore conditional on the correlation. (printed 2-88 to 2-94, PDF 113 to 119.)
Bed-to-bed uniformity was good: 49 RS loose beds, four drops each, mean Gp 11.76 plus or minus 0.14 g at 95 percent confidence on the means. (printed 2-90, PDF 115.)
Static penetrometers (a pocket penetrometer and a cone proving-ring penetrometer) were tried and rejected because results varied greatly between operators. There is no static penetrometer data in this report. (printed 2-94, PDF 119.)

title: Appendix C envelopes checked against their own data sheets
text:
Note



Review status: pending. Written from a first read of the pages; quote with that caveat until the page transcriptions are reconciled.


Source: AM-68-1 Vol. II (NASA CR-92215), Appendix C. Every failure envelope (Figs. C-1A to C-7A) plots the peak shear stresses of the direct shear tests on the data sheets that follow it. With both read independently and reconciled (batches curves-appc-b1 to -b6), each envelope point can be compared with the peak of its own test. Findings, 2026-10-14:

Fig. C-2A (PS soil, printed C-6, PDF 120) has its legend swapped. As printed, the squares are the loose group (Dr .33 to .53) on the steeper 49.5-degree line and the circles the dense group (Dr 1.15 to 1.3) on the 46.7-degree line, which would make loose PS stronger than dense. The squares are within 8 to 48 psf of the peaks of the dense tests (Fig. C-2C, printed C-8, PDF 122) and 150 to 770 psf from the loose ones (Fig. C-2B, printed C-7, PDF 121); the circles are within 4 to 54 psf of the loose peaks. Fig. C-17 (printed C-39, PDF 153) plots 46.7 degrees at the loose Dr. Loose PS: 46.7 degrees; dense PS: 49.5 degrees. The records b68-ds-fc-2a-dr33-53 and b68-ds-fc-2a-dr115-130 carry the corrected pairing; the printed legend text is kept as printed.
Fig. C-4A (RC2, printed C-12, PDF 126): two points of the dense group sit 150 to 200 psf below the peaks of the corresponding tests of Fig. C-4C (printed C-14, PDF 128), in both readings; a difference within the report, not a reading error. The other envelope points sit 10 to 46 psf above the sheets’ peaks (the envelopes are drafted on tick-only axes; part of the offset is the drafting of their scales).
Fig. C-1A (RS, printed C-2, PDF 116): three symbols sit on another group’s line (a filled circle at 315 psf on the 45.5-degree dashed extension, the triangle at zero normal stress, a filled circle at 1772 psf on the 51-degree line); their peaks identify them as tests of Figs. C-1C and C-1D, so the drawn lines pass through symbols of other groups near the axis. The triangle at zero normal stress is the zero-stress test of C-1D (476 psf), which Fig. C-9A’s printed fit (tan 1.3059, cohesion 634.20 psf) also includes.
Fig. C-6A (LSM, printed C-17, PDF 131) prints no friction angles and no line labels. Its groups are identified by the data sheets (batch curves-appc-b6, both readings): the circles are the loose tests of Fig. C-6B (printed C-18, PDF 132), within 4 to 35 psf of their peaks; the squares the dense tests of Fig. C-6C (printed C-19, PDF 133), within 5 to 51 psf; the triangles the tests of Fig. C-6D (printed C-20, PDF 134), 24 to 90 psf below their peaks. A mark one reader took for an unlisted downward triangle at 2946 psf is the circle of the 2934 psf test of C-6B (18 psf from its peak). The dense group’s line is the flattest of the three; that is in the data sheets themselves (dense peaks 3019 psf at 3815 psf and 4018 at 4695, against 3756 and 4252 for the loose group), not a reading error.
Fig. C-6C prints its second test as 1961 psf; Fig. C-6A plots it at about 1740 psf. The envelope’s square sits at a normal stress of 1739 to 1742 psf (both readings) with the C-6C peak to 1 psf (1398 against 1399). The other LSM sheets use 1761 psf (and C-6C its own 714 psf for the lightest test). Either the legend’s 1961 or the envelope’s position is a drafting slip; the pages do not say which. The record keeps 1961 as printed.
Fig. C-5A (SS, printed C-15, PDF 129): only the first group (circles, Dr .02 to .13) has data sheets here (Fig. C-5B, printed C-16, PDF 130). Three circles are within 25 psf of their tests’ peaks; the 734 psf one sits 55 psf above it and the 3815 psf one 104 psf below it, in both readings. The other three groups come from Bendix Report No. MM-65-2 (as printed on the figure; the figures index read MM-66-2) and cannot be checked here.
Fig. C-7A (RSM-b, printed C-21, PDF 135): every symbol is within 0.4 psi of the peak of its test (dotted circles: Fig. C-7C, Dr 0.53; dotted triangles: Fig. C-7B, Dr 1.0).

Use: when quoting a friction angle or cohesion of these soils from Appendix C, take the group from the data sheets, not from the printed legend of C-2A. Cite as AM-68-1 Vol. II, Fig. C-2A, printed C-6, PDF 120 with this note.

text: How the data are organized and how agents and people work on them. These pages are the repository’s own documents, rendered as they are.

title: Methods
section: The two-agent method in one paragraph
text:
The two-agent method in one paragraph
Every inventory or extraction is made twice, by Claude and by Codex, each from the same evidence (the PDF, the page map, the agreed indexes) and without seeing the other’s output. A script compares the two mechanically; cells that match are agreed; cells that differ are settled by a documented rule, a convention, or a re-read of the page, and the resolution is written down with credit to whichever reading was right. Agreement between two agents is not confirmation: a student reviews every disagreement and audits a 5 to 10 percent sample of agreements, and only recorded audits count (qa/audits.csv).

Values are SI; the printed-unit values and the pixel coordinates on the page image are kept beside them so every point can be checked against the scan. x_read_bound and y_read_bound are reading bounds in printed units: the largest change of value over the point’s pixel interval on the piecewise map, plus the location error of the two lines around it (D-025; the global calibration residual is not added, see qa//calibration-sensitivity.md for the affine difference); x_bound_si and y_bound_si are the same in SI. They are not standard deviations.

title: Simulate a test
text: How to set up a virtual experiment of a test in this collection and compare it with the measurement, worked through on one test. The steps do not depend on the simulator, and no simulation result is shown. The example is load-penetration test LPT 24, chosen because its record gives the density of the bed, the tool, the bin and the loading rate.

title: Simulate a test
text:
1. Choose a test
Find a test lists every test. In a load-penetration test a tool is pushed into a prepared bed of soil and the load on it is recorded against depth. In LPT 24, a cylinder 101.6 mm (4 in) in diameter was pushed at 0.423 mm/s into dense red scoria (RS) with a bulk density of 825 kg/m³.

title: Simulate a test
text:
2. Read its virtual experiment card
The card on the test’s page lists what the report gives about the soil, the bed, the tool, the motion and the measurement, and what it leaves out. Each value is marked reported, soil reference or left to the user, and each citation opens the page of the report it comes from.

title: Simulate a test
text:
3. Gather the soil properties
The Soils page gives the report’s soil table. The row that matches this test is soil No. 4, RS Dense: mean grain size (D50) 1.8 mm, friction angle 47.3 degrees and modulus 75.2 MPa. These values belong to the soil’s nominal state, relative density (Dr) 0.80 and 810.5 kg/m³; the bed of this test is denser, 825 kg/m³. Two cautions follow. Properties that depend on density are read at the bed’s own state where the report allows it: it plots friction angle against relative density (AM-68-1 Vol. I, Fig. 2-23, printed 2-46, PDF 71). And the modulus was measured with sound waves; the report warns that static and wave-based moduli can differ by an order of magnitude (AM-68-1 Vol. II, Appendix B, printed 1, PDF 104), so it is a reference, not a static stiffness.

title: Simulate a test
text:
4. Build the geometry
From the card: the bin is 0.457 m wide, 0.914 m long and 0.914 m deep, of plywood with a glass front; the cylinder is 101.6 mm in diameter, its axis 229 mm from the nearest wall, and starts at the soil surface; gravity is 9.81456 m/s², the report’s value for Earth, 32.2 ft/s², converted exactly (glossary, printed 2-2, PDF 27). The bin is part of the test. The report found that tests of the same soil in larger bins tended to reach higher peak loads (AM-68-1 Vol. I, printed 2-74, PDF 99), and that in one test in dense sand a failure plane reached the glass front of this bin (printed 2-59, PDF 84). A model that makes the bin smaller to save computing time has to show that this does not change the load.

title: Simulate a test
section: 5. Choose the missing inputs and bracket them
text:
5. Choose the missing inputs and bracket them
Every input marked as left to the user needs a value. For each one, choose a plausible low and a plausible high value, run the virtual experiment at both, and report the spread of the result next to the result itself. For this test the card lists:

Fill depth: not printed. The procedure fills the box in stages and weighs the bed at six volume marks up to the full box (13.78 cubic feet, 0.390 m³) to check that its density is uniform.
How the bed was placed and compacted: not printed for this test. The dense beds of these tests were generally made with a vibratory plate compactor, three passes per layer about 76 mm (3 in) thick, giving relative densities of 0.85 to 0.95.
The zero of penetration: the printed load leaves zero at 1.3 mm; whether the cylinder touched the surface there or at zero is not stated.
Relative density of this bed: not printed. The tests of Fig. 2-44, this one among them, average about 0.96. Read at this bed’s density on the report’s density chart for the soil, it is about 0.90 (0.82 to above 1 within the chart’s 95 percent limits). The soil table’s 0.80 belongs to the soil’s nominal state, not to this bed.
Soil strength at this bed’s density: the report plots friction angle against relative density.
Cohesion: a bearing-capacity interpretation in the report, not a measured input. It found that the apparent cohesion of its shear tests predicts higher bearing loads than observed, and that about 0.7 kPa (0.1 psi), some 50 times less, explains some of the size effects in these tests.
The cylinder’s end shape, length, material and surface, and where it stood along the bin: not printed.
Friction between the soil and the cylinder, and between the soil and the walls (plywood, glass): not reported.
Any model parameter the report does not measure, such as a static stiffness or the properties of grains.

A worked example: the relative density of this bed. The report’s average for the tests of Fig. 2-44 is about 0.96 (AM-68-1 Vol. I, printed 2-74, PDF 99). Reading this bed’s density, 8.09 kN/m³ (51.5 pcf), on the report’s density chart for the soil (AM-68-1 Vol. II, Fig. A-3, printed A-7, PDF 8) gives about 0.90 on the mean curve, and 0.82 to above 1 within its 95 percent confidence limits. The two sources do not agree exactly, so a bracket of 0.82 to 0.96, with 0.90 as a baseline, is one defensible choice; the soil strength at each end is then read at that relative density.

title: Simulate a test
section: 6. Decide the output and the loading speed
text:
6. Decide the output and the loading speed
Record the quantity that was measured: the axial force the soil exerts on the cylinder (what the load cell read) against the cylinder’s penetration below the original soil surface. The printed curve covers 1.3 to 74.0 mm; the test itself went further, but the figure does not show how far. State where the zero of force and of penetration are, and whether the cylinder’s weight is included. The test ran at 0.423 mm/s. A faster virtual push saves computing time, but it has to be shown not to change the load, for example by running two speeds and comparing.

title: Simulate a test
text:
7. Compare with the measurement
Download the measured points from the test’s page: penetration and load in SI, each with its reading bound, the precision with which the printed figure could be read.
A worked example. The first peak of the measured curve is the point at 22.6 mm and 4,018 N, read to within 0.54 mm and 21 N. A simulated curve is compared with it at the same penetration, by interpolating the simulated force there. A difference smaller than the reading bound cannot be told apart from a reading error; a larger one still has to be weighed against how much tests on similar beds differ, which the reading bound does not include.
The report gives no repeat of this test. The other tests printed in the same figure ran on other beds, at other rates or densities, so the spread between them mixes those differences with the test-to-test scatter and gives only a rough idea of it.

title: Simulate a test
text:
8. Keep related records together
When some tests are used to tune a model and others to check it, three kinds of relation keep records on the same side: two printings of one test (LPT 24 is printed in Fig. 2-42 and Fig. 2-44: one test, not two); a result derived from tests, such as a failure envelope drawn from several shear tests; and tests run on one shared bed, where the report says so. Tests that only share a figure, a soil or a bin size are neighbors for comparison, not dependencies. Each test’s page lists both.

title: Simulate a test
text:
9. Share it
A script that runs a virtual experiment of a test hosted here is welcome; the Contribute page says what it should state.
